Basal metabolic rate in the Trinidad spiny pocket mouse (Heteromys anomalus) was assessed through respirometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions, revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 100.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 100.5 milliliters per hour] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This elevated metabolic rate, characteristic of heteromyid rodents adapted to warm environments, underscores the high energetic costs associated with maintaining homeothermy in this species. In parallel, reproductive output was quantified in a captive colony maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], where females were observed to produce litters containing 3 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 to 4 pups per litter], a modest fecundity per event that aligns with the general reproductive strategy of related heteromyids. The frequency of these reproductive events was recorded as approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year], a rate that reflects the species' capacity for sustained breeding under favorable thermal regimes when food resources remain abundant throughout the year.

Neonatal mass at parturition in Heteromys anomalus has been estimated based on data from the closely related congener Heteromys salvini, with newborn pups weighing approximately 1.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.9 grams]. This relatively low birth weight is typical of altricial rodent neonates, which undergo a substantial proportion of their somatic growth after emergence from the uterus. The gestation period, also inferred from Heteromys salvini given the scarcity of direct observations in H. anomalus, spans 27 days [tg = 27 days] when females are maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This gestational duration is comparable to that documented in other small-bodied heteromyids and reflects a developmental tempo that balances the energetic demands of embryogenesis with the mother's capacity to sustain a pregnancy under warm environmental conditions. The placental transfer of nutrients during this period supports the formation of a relatively undeveloped neonate that is heavily dependent upon maternal care immediately following live birth.

Lactation and the subsequent transition to nutritional independence are critical phases in the early ontogeny of this species. Weaning, the point at which the suckling juvenile ceases to rely on the mother's milk and begins to consume solid food, occurs at approximately 29 days after birth [tx = approximately 29 days after birth] in individuals maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a value extrapolated from data on Heteromys salvini. This relatively brief nursing period is consistent with the rapid developmental trajectory observed in tropical rodents, where accelerated growth is advantageous in environments with high predation pressure. During the pre-weaning interval, the altricial neonate undergoes a phase of intense mass gain fueled by the mother's lipid-rich milk, transitioning from a highly dependent pup into a weaned juvenile capable of independent foraging. The temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C] represents the typical thermal condition under which these developmental milestones were recorded in captivity.

The timing of reproductive maturation in Heteromys anomalus has been documented under captive conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], with puberty—defined as the attainment of gonadal activity and the capacity to reproduce—achieved approximately 50 days after birth [tp = approximately 50 days after birth]. This rapid onset of sexual maturity is noteworthy among heteromyid rodents and likely reflects an adaptive response to the relatively stable, warm climates of Trinidad, where seasonal constraints on breeding are minimal. Female ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass attained by reproductively mature individuals, has been recorded at 69.3 grams [Wwi = 69.3 grams]. This body size is comparable to that of other members of the genus Heteromys and is associated with a life history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction and relatively small litter sizes. The interplay between the timing of pubertal development and adult body mass suggests that females allocate resources toward achieving a threshold size before initiating reproductive effort.

Longevity data from captive populations maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C] indicate that the maximum lifespan of Heteromys anomalus reaches approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years], a duration that is relatively extended for a rodent of its body size. This comparatively slow pace of life, with a moderate lifespan coupled with a modest annual reproductive output of approximately 1 litter per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 litter per year] (each containing 3 to 4 pups, as noted previously), situates the Trinidad spiny pocket mouse within a slow-fast life history continuum that is intermediate between short-lived, highly fecund murids and the longer-lived, less fecund heteromyids of arid regions. A female weighing 69.3 grams [Wwi = 69.3 grams] sustaining such a reproductive schedule over nearly five years faces substantial cumulative energetic demands, particularly during gestation and lactation. The basal metabolic rate of 100.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 100.5 milliliters per hour] measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] provides a baseline for understanding the energetic underpinnings of this life history strategy.
